topicName: Query Optimization and N+1 Problem (Includes, Joins, Preload)
content:
[{"order":1,"type":"heading","text":"Query Optimization and the N+1 Problem in Ruby on Rails"},{"order":2,"type":"paragraph","text":"One of the most common performance bottlenecks in Ruby on Rails applications is the infamous N+1 query problem. This tutorial explores how this issue occurs, how to identify it, and how to resolve it efficiently using Includes, Joins, and Preload."},{"order":3,"type":"heading","text":"Understanding the N+1 Query Problem"},{"order":4,"type":"paragraph","text":"The N+1 query problem occurs when your code executes one initial query to retrieve the parent records (1), and then executes N additional queries to retrieve the associated child records for each of the N parents. This severely degrades database performance."},{"order":5,"type":"subheading","text":"The Anti-Pattern Example"},{"order":6,"type":"code","text":"# Controller
@posts = Post.all

# View
<% @posts.each do |post| %>
  <%= post.title %>
  <%= post.user.name %>
<% end %>"},{"order":7,"type":"paragraph","text":"If you have 100 posts, the above code triggers 1 query to fetch all posts, and 100 separate queries to fetch the user for each post. Total: 101 queries."},{"order":8,"type":"heading","text":"Solution 1: Active Record Includes"},{"order":9,"type":"paragraph","text":"The includes method is the most common way to solve the N+1 problem. It loads the associations using either eager_load (a single LEFT OUTER JOIN query) or preload (two separate queries), depending on whether you are querying conditions on the association."},{"order":10,"type":"code","text":"@posts = Post.includes(:user)"},{"order":11,"type":"heading","text":"Solution 2: Active Record Preload"},{"order":12,"type":"paragraph","text":"The preload method always loads associations using a separate query. It loads the primary records first, then queries the associated records using an IN clause. This prevents complex join table bloat when dealing with large has_many associations."},{"order":13,"type":"code","text":"@posts = Post.preload(:comments)"},{"order":14,"type":"heading","text":"Solution 3: Active Record Joins"},{"order":15,"type":"paragraph","text":"The joins method performs an INNER JOIN on the tables. Unlike includes and preload, joins does not load the associated records into memory. It is primarily used for filtering records based on associations rather than preventing the N+1 problem for data rendering."},{"order":16,"type":"code","text":"@posts = Post.joins(:comments).where(comments: { approved: true })"},{"order":17,"type":"heading","text":"Summary of Best Practices"},{"order":18,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Use includes when you need to load associations and want Rails to automatically decide between eager loading or preloading."},{"order":19,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Use preload when you specifically want separate queries to avoid massive JOIN overhead on large has_many relationships."},{"order":20,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Use joins strictly for database filtering and querying, not for avoiding N+1 view rendering issues."},{"order":21,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Enable the bullet gem in your development environment to automatically detect and alert you to N+1 queries."}]
